subsubtopic: ALLEGED IMPORTATION OF UNITED STATES WELDERS INTO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Minister of Labour whether he is in a position today to give a reply to my question of last Friday concerning the importation of United States welders into British Columbia to work on the Westcoast Transmission line?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS
subsubtopic: ALLEGED IMPORTATION OF UNITED STATES WELDERS INTO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the hon. member for Vancouver East and others have raised this point.
On the subject of the complaint from the British Columbia welders' association regarding the entry of 14 welders from the United States, our regional office of the unemployment insurance commission in Vancouver is keeping in close touch with this situation and has worked closely with the immigration branch, to which employers must first apply

for the admission of various workers into Canada. The immigration branch in turn gets in touch with the national employment service to ascertain whether or not Canadian workers are available who are able to do the work concerned, and only if they are unable to recruit the skilled workers needed are American workers admitted to Canada.
The united association of plumbers and pipe fitters, who hold a collective agreement with the pipe-line contractors, the British Columbia office of the unemployment insurance commission and the immigration branch considered that the employers' requests for stringer-bead men for front end crews were genuine, as it is not always possible at the moment to find in Canada a sufficient number of stringer-bead men.
I think I should say, Mr. Speaker, that this type of employee, namely the stringer-bead man, is the ultimate as a welder. He starts the weld at the joint and it is most important that this start be made faultlessly. The joint must be firm and exact, and it requires highly experienced men to effect it. Less experienced welders complete the joint started by the stringer-bead man who continues on to start the next joint. Thus, for every two stringer-bead men employed, 12 to 18 other welders are required. Our office was unable to find sufficient bead men who were able to meet the rigid test required for this operation and, as a consequence, the 14 welders in question were allowed in from the United States.
Our regional office made a study of the various companies presently employing welders and found that, of a total of 79, 66 are Canadians and 13 Americans.
All the pipe-line contractors are still field testing welders and building up their crews for maximum activity. It is anticipated that in the weeks to come all qualified Canadian welders will be employed either on the main line, the feeder lines or on municipal distribution systems.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in speaking to the resolution I pointed out that three of the sections are amendments to the Defence Services Pension Act and nine are amendments to the National Defence Act. As the sections are not related to each other nor do they all deal with one subject I assume that we shall not be able to discuss the principle of the bill as is usual on second reading. Canadian Forces Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we move into committee and come to the detailed discussion in relation to the various sections of this bill, I should like to comment on the manner in which the bill is now being introduced to the house. It is typical of the blundering and panicky way in which the government has been conducting its business all throughout this session. The resolution preceding this bill was placed on the order paper on January 12, five calendar months ago today. There it remained until yesterday afternoon, when the resolution was briefly discussed. The minister made a short statement and I asked a question or two. I was told that there were several amendments and that the sections were not related, as the minister has said today.
There are 13 different sections in this bill. They deal with amendments to two different acts, namely the Defence Services Pension Act and the National Defence Act. The National Defence Act has been amended several times, and in order to understand at least one of the sections of the bill it will be necessary to refer to the amendments which have been made to the National Defence Act. In addition to that consideration, in the bill and the notes attached to the various clauses reference is made to the United Kingdom act, the new Criminal Code of Canada and the Penitentiary Act. In order to study various clauses properly, those acts all must be referred to.
This bill was given first reading yesterday afternoon. At the close of yesterday's sitting the Minister of Finance said that if the bill was not already printed, it would be available early this morning. I arrived here and cleared my mail box at nine o'clock. There was no bill in it. Since I thought it would be discussed today I went down again just before the committee on external affairs met at eleven o'clock. There was no bill there then. I remained in the committee on external affairs until lunch time. I had my lunch, and then I found this bill.
That certainly is trying to railroad things through this house. I do not know whether other members have studied the bill. I have looked through it, and I shall do the best I can to offer some comments from time to time on the various sections. In view of the very limited time that hon. members have had, I do think we have the right to expect a full and detailed statement by the Minister of National Defence on the various clauses. We have not had the time to give them the proper consideration that we normally do. I feel that I am not coming to
[Mr. Campney.l
the discussion of this bill prepared in the way I usually am with any comments I have to make on the actions of this government. If, therefore, my questions may not be strictly relevant it will be for that reason, and I shall ask for some latitude in that respect.
Again I draw attention to the fact that for five months this resolution remained on the order paper and then in less than 24 hours- less than five hours, in fact-after we have received the bill we are asked to discuss it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: If the minister speaks now he will close the debate.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
It will be too bad if the minister closes the debate, because we have not started. I must join with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich in offering a protest against the method of introducing this bill in this house with such great haste. It has just come to my attention now in the bills which have been filed on our desks by the page boys and I have not had time to read it over. Under such circumstances the minister can hardly expect the best of co-operation in getting the bill through this house.
We have protested in other years against this method of bringing in an omnibus bill which amends more than one statute. This time I notice the minister says that this amending bill deals with just two statutes instead of the half dozen statutes that were amended last year. But it is wrong to do it this way, and I think we shall continue to protest as vigorously as we can against this method. We make a further protest against bringing the thing in as rapidly as this when there was plenty of time to have the bill printed and in our hands long ago.
This is the type of bill that requires careful study because the matters dealt with, particularly in the amendments which deal with the code of service discipline, require close attention. If we hastily pass this through we may be putting into the code of service discipline something which should not be there. How the minister expects us to understand this bill with the very limited explanation that he has given I do not know. I think he should have taken his time and at the resolution stage yesterday given a much more detailed statement as to the amendments which were to be introduced, and today he might very well have spoken at some length on the matter.
To approach a bill of this nature in this frame of mind is not conducive to its passage in short order, and I would hope that the minister would take note of our feelings in

the matter and when on any other occasion he has to introduce an amending bill in this house he will do so differently.
We faced this problem last year and the year before. How can you discuss the principle of a bill when it amends two statutes? What is the principle? Do you divide it into two parts and say there are two principles in this bill, or how do you approach the subject? At this stage if we go into the question of the clauses I am sure we will be informed that that is not an orderly procedure, and that should be taken up at the committee stage. But that is the problem we are faced with this afternoon. A hastily introduced measure which is of an omnibus character does not lend itself to a discussion of the principle involved.
Then the minister in his introductory remarks has not been helpful. According to the information I have before me, in his statement yesterday at the resolution stage he just touched on the various amendments that were being brought before us without more than a sentence or two of explanation. For example, where the amendments deal with persons accompanying a unit to whom the commander may issue orders, he does not tell us what types of persons he has in mind, and I would certainly want to know that before I could comment upon it. There are persons who are subject to the code of service discipline, yet apparently they are not actually in uniform. According to this amendment the commander of the unit will be able to issue orders to them to take certain action under certain circumstances. Well, what type of person is involved in that?
Then the restriction that is to be imposed on drivers of vehicles who are considered to be impaired might have merited greater explanation than the minister offered. What is the standard of evidence that is going to be required with regard to this matter of impairment, either due to the use of alcohol or a drug? What drug, for example, is being considered? Then what has required the necessity for a further amendment, or an amendment, with regard to the enforcement of discipline in service prisons and detention barracks? I presume these things arise because of something that has to be corrected. Well, why did the minister not tell us what has to be corrected? What is wrong now with the code of service discipline that necessitates an amendment respecting the enforcement of discipline in service prisons and in detention barracks?
Then there is his amendment with respect to service vehicles paying tolls on bridges, highways and canals. What is being done
Canadian Forces Act
at the present time? He did not give us any explanation of that; and so it goes. The minister does not deserve to have this bill given second reading this afternoon. As the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich pointed out, we have not had time to look at the thing very carefully; we have not had time to get the statutes and the amendments of recent years and compare these new amendments with what is already on the statute books and put them in their proper places, with the result that we cannot discuss the question with the care and attention that a matter of this kind deserves.

Mr. Speaker, I rise just to support the protest that has been made by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre with respect to the form of this bill. This is a protest that these hon. gentlemen and some of us have been making for four or five years now. I do not know how many years we are going to have to keep on making the protest before the practice is changed; but it does seem to me it would be far more logical, when the government wishes to ask parliament to amend the Defence Services Pension Act, to bring before parliament a bill amending that act; also, when it wishes to amend the National Defence Act, to bring before parliament a bill amending the National Defence Act.
This practice that has been followed now for several years of bringing in a bill entitled the Canadian Forces Act in which are included amendments to a number of different acts-only two this year, but in other years there have been a number

seems to me to be an illogical and shall I say sloppy way of dealing with the matter. I think it would be far better if on this occasion the government would consider the proposal that has been made from this side of the house, namely that these acts be treated on their own and amended by separate bills amending each act by itself.
I have made that plea on a number of occasions. As I say, it seems to have fallen on deaf ears. I feel it is with justification that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre have made this protest once again today.

There is always the cumulative index in each annual volume of statutes where most people who look for bills can generally find them. I think the advantage to the services of having one bill each year covering matters that deal particularly and specifically with them has been of great benefit, in that it provides a means of quick reference and a means of getting the new changes known quickly, both of which are of advantage generally in the administration of the services.
As I have said, the sections of the bill are completely independent of each other. I think that is why in all previous cases- and I would like to suggest in this case also- it has been found that the practical and realistic way of dealing with them is to pass second reading of the bill and then take each section by itself in committee and discuss it at length, at least to the extent that hon. members wish to discuss it. This is of course the Defence Services Pension Act. The minister is aware of the fact that on a good many occasions both in this house and in committee I have raised a point with respect to this act. I notice that despite the amendments before us the matter I raised has not been taken care of.
What I had in mind is this. A member of the forces who contributes to the superannuation fund may die while in the service. Perhaps he has paid into that pension fund for 14 or 15 years. After he passes away in the service his contributions are then returned to his wife or his dependents. When that contribution is returned the income tax department will make an assessment against the total contribution-it may be $3,000 or $4,000-and they will tax it. I know of one case where a young officer contributed for 10 years and there was a sum of $600 deducted by the income tax department from the contribution when it was returned to his wife. I think it is a pretty rank piece of injustice, and for four or five years now I have been bringing it to the attention of the minister, and I did so in committee when the defence act was amended a few years ago.
I believe the department is being lax. That is a matter which is much more important, I think, than any amendment that is contained in the present act. It merely involves making arrangements with the income tax department. The superannuation contribution that is returned to the widow of a man who died in the service is not income because he has already paid income tax on his salary while he was in the service. Of course he would be allowed to offset that contribution, but the contribution is perhaps the only thing the widow has to depend on in the future, and I do not think it could be considered as income.

Canadian Forces Act
I wonder if the minister has taken the matter up with the Minister of National Revenue. I myself have done so. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: I hoped perhaps the minister would have given an explanation of the advantages and purpose of this particular amendment. As far as I can understand, if an officer is offered and does not accept a further fixed term of employment, then he is compulsorily retired. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
This section is to take care of an officer who has risen from the ranks and has taken a fixed term commission. At the expiry of the fixed term he may be granted a permanent commission or he may be released entirely or he may have his fixed term commission extended, as is often the case. Under the act as it stands if at the completion of his fixed term he is offered but does not accept an extension of his fixed term commission he is deemed to have voluntarily retired. Therefore he gets only the gratuities payable under the pay regulations for his service during his period as an officer, but he loses any gratuities he might have as the result of his service as a man in the ranks.
In addition to clarifying the law as it exists, this section takes care of that situation and enables a man who has risen from the ranks and who has proceeded in the manner I have outlined to get a gratuity based on his service as an officer and as a man in the ranks. In other words it works to his advantage.

speechtext:
That raises the whole question of debts incurred by servicemen. If the services themselves are going to assume the right to collect a debt which is owing to the service by a man in the forces, should consideration not be given to the collection of debts which are owed to civilians by men who are in the services? I regret to say that from time to time there are men in the services who do not meet their civilian obligations. They escape paying their debts either by transfer or by the mere fact that they remain in the unit or retire on pension, and the civilian land owner or person who has rented accommodation to them or the man who has sold them a television set on time and so on cannot collect. Recently, as the minister knows, the bar association of British Columbia passed a resolution which I presume has been brought to his attention. It reads in part as follows:
Whereas many merchants and others through dealing with persons in the employ and pay of the government of Canada, by giving to them credit, have suffered hardship and in many cases grievous loss because advantage is taken by such persons of the fact that their wages or salaries cannot be garnisheed-
Then it goes on to recommend that service personnel and other personnel in the employ of the government should come under the various provincial acts which govern these circumstances. There are not a great many cases so far as the armed forces are concerned, but there are a limited number. These men who do not live up to their obligations bring discredit to their ships or their units. If the government is now bringing in an amendment so as to be able to collect debts owing to the government, should the government not also consider providing some relief for those unfortunate persons who have been victimized by persons in the services who have not lived up to the traditions of the service, are not a credit to the service, and who may have gone on pension? It seems to me that if this is suitable procedure for the government for the collection of debts, then there should be an obligation on the government to see that debts owing to civilians are paid.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
The pay account of a man in the services has always been regarded by the services, and I presume by the man himself, as a private matter between the two parties, the paying party and the receiving

party. To open up that position to the extent of allowing the paymaster to deduct alleged debts owing to other people would certainly be initiating a new principle, particularly if this practice were extended to the civil service. There may be some reasons why at first blush it would seem to be a desirable thing, but I am sure that on second thought my hon. friend will realize that it would hardly be practicable, and certainly would not make for good relations between the man and his employer, the government service.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Has this resolution of the bar association been brought to the minister's attention?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Yes. As a matter of fact we have received representations from time to time, as I presume those concerned with the administration of the civil service have, from interested bodies, I think that has been going on for quite a while. However, it is a very large subject and a very novel approach which, so far as X know, has not been accepted in any government circles, either civil or military.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
I should like to add my voice to that of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. I do not know whether it should be suggested that we are asking the government to act in any way as a collection agency, but certainly the brief that has been referred to has suggested that members of the armed forces should be placed in the same category as any civilians in connection with their civil obligations. At this time I do not think we should simply put the matter off by saying that in the past there has been a well-recognized principle.
It may be that in times of national emergency it would cause considerable dislocation in the armed forces to have the personnel subject to garnishee or attachment in some way for civilian debts, but in times such as these there would appear to be no reason why the same obligations should not be shouldered by these people as are shouldered by everyone else in the country. I strongly suggest that we do not rest this case simply on the basis of an old principle. As the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich has said, it brings no credit on the armed forces if there are people in the forces who avoid their obligations.
I think the vast majority of the people in the forces, no matter what branch they might be in, would be quite satisfied to see some change in this type of regulation. As I have said before, I do not think we should suggest that the paymaster become a collection agency; but if the government is prepared 67509-314i
Canadian Forces Act
to take steps to protect its own position, as it is here, it should be willing to recognize the same principle on a broader basis.
As to the section itself, may I say this. It seems to me that here is an example of the lazy-man approach. If there is any credit left in the account of the person receiving the pay or the pension, obviously it is going to be necessary for the department to track that person down in order to make the payment; but it would appear that it would be much easier, if it is simply the case of a deduction, to send him notice of it. We are removing from the person who might be considered a defendant considerable of his rights in the first part of the section when we say that the governor in council by regulation may prescribe the manner in which this money can be collected. What excuse is there to take the next step and say "We can just send you notice of it by registered post"?
I do not know whether this is the ordinary type of contra-account transaction we have where we say, "We have $10 of yours, you owe us $5 and we are sending you on $5". But in any case it would appear that the combination expressed in the first part of the section and the second removes the opportunity for the man to put in his defence and say, "I do not owe you this money and I am not going to pay you until you prove it". Under this regulation the department simply has to say, "You owe this money, we have deducted it and that is what you have left".

Clause agreed to.
On clause 5-Subordinate officers and men.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
We now come to the consideration of the amendments to the National Defence Act. In the notes with respect to clause 5 I see the following:
This clause would permit the enrolment of a subordinate officer in the Canadian forces for either an indefinite or a fixed term of service . . .
Are they permitted to change from one to the other? Can a person who starts off on a fixed term change at his request to an indefinite term?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
Generally speaking, if an officer starts off on a fixed term commission, he is working up to a permanent commission later on. This amendment deals with a particular type of officer known as a subordinate officer. I understand that a subordinate officer in the navy is an acting sublieutenant or a midshipman or a naval cadet; in the army he is an officer cadet; and in the air force he is a flight cadet. He is enrolled but not commissioned, although he is looked upon when he is enrolled as being a proper candidate, subject to check as his activities

Canadian Forces Act
go on, for a commission. Under the act as it now stands a subordinate officer can enrol only for a fixed term. The amendment provided by this clause would permit him to enrol either for an indefinite term or for a fixed term as at present. In other words it gives him wider latitude than he has under the law as it now stands.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: That did not quite answer my question. I asked whether he would be able to change from enrolment for a fixed term into enrolment for an indefinite term. For instance, I have in mind a cadet at the H.M.C.S. Venture college at Esquimalt, who would be there for a fixed term of so many years. Could he during the period of that service change to an indefinite period?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Only with the consent of the service concerned.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: It would be given, if it were given, after some period of observation as to his likelihood of becoming a successful officer.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
Would the minister say why subclause 3 has been eliminated? In the present act paragraph 3 reads:
(3) A person under the age of 18 years shall not be enrolled without the consent of one of his parents or of his guardian.
That paragraph has been eliminated from the new amendment?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: No. Subclause 3 is not being eliminated. The amendment that is made is just being made to subclause 2. Subclause 1 of section 21 and subclause 3 remain as they were.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: They remain?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Yes.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 6-Persons deemed to be under .command of superior officer.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Before I make any remarks about this clause, may I say that I assume it covers people whether they are affiliated with the armed forces in Canada, within the jurisdiction here or in a foreign jurisdiction. Would that be right? Is that a proper assumption?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
This section practically
speaking, applies only outside of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
Perhaps that answer limits my remarks to a certain extent, but I am wondering whether the department has taken into account the fact that the use of nuclear weapons may necessitate the

officer commanding having authority not only over those affiliated with the armed forces, as set out here, but that his authority perhaps-although some question of sovereignty may arise in connection with my remarks-[DOT] may necessitate his having control over all the persons within an area and, in so far as our act is concerned, that he should be protected in connection with orders to remove all civilians within a certain area. Perhaps we cannot get around any liability which he might have in a foreign jurisdiction but certainly we should be able to provide that he is protected, in so far as our own armed forces are concerned, if he orders all civilians out of a certain area. This section would not appear to take that situation into account.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
This section has nothing to do with civilians generally as a class. It has to do only with those within the definition of persons accompanying a unit outside of Canada. They have already been made subject to the code of service discipline but, under the law as it now stands, they have not been made subject to the orders of the commander of the unit to which they may be attached or which they may be accompanying. The purpose of this amendment is to give him some authority in certain cases.
These things take place, of course, in potential war areas. The idea is to give the commanding officer authority to take them under his command for purposes of defence and evacuation except as regards bearing arms. In other words, he could move them out of there or move them about for these purposes other than for active service in the sense of engaging in the bearing of arms. It is just a small gap that was found in the general law which provided that something could be done but did not provide who could do it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: I wonder whether the minister could help us out here. Who are these people who are subject to the code of service discipline by virtue of the paragraphs that are mentioned here? Would the minister refresh our memories on that point?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Well, principally, of course, they will be dependents together with other civilians who for certain reasons would be accompanying the unit. The definition covers persons who participate with a unit or other element of the service in carrying out any of its movements, manoeuvres, duties, warlike operations, and so on. It would go no farther than those categories, plus the dependents of the members of the unit. These two general classes cover practically all cases.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: May I ask whether I heard the minister correctly when he said this applied only to persons accompanying Canadian forces out of Canada? Where is that contained? I do not see it in subsection 8 of section 56 of the National Defence Act, as amended.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: It was covered in the 1954 amendment. Subsection 7 (a) of section 56 defines persons accompanying the Canadian forces, and if I recollect correctly I think it deals only with dependents accompanying them out of Canada. Subsection 7 (a) of section 56, subclause (c), which defines classes of persons accompanying Canadian forces as, "a dependent out of Canada or of any officer or man serving beyond Canada in the unit", and so on.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: That would not apply to any personnel who might be in the northern parts of Canada?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 7-Parties to an offence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: I have not had an opportunity of looking at the Criminal Code. Can the minister give assurance that this conforms exactly to the wording of the Criminal Code?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Yes, it does, Mr. Chairman. The new Criminal Code changes a little the results which flow from common intention in respect of offences under the code, and we have made the same changes in respect of service offences. I think the amendment is identical, word for word, with the Criminal Code.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Would the minister answer this question. With respect to personnel serving outside of the country, what law is taken into account in defining "unlawful purpose"?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: I think an unlawful purpose would be defined as under the Canadian Criminal Code in respect of Canadians, or under the National Defence Act, where we have our own code of service discipline which we administer whether at home or abroad.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Would this not include any civilian law of the locality where the armed forces are serving?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
Only to the extent that the National Defence Act makes an offence against the local law an offence under the National Defence Act. If the National Defence Act, as it does in some cases, makes the law of the place applicable, then the jurisdiction rests under the National Defence Act, but it would have to be within the limit of the provisions of that act.
Canadian Forces Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
I have only one observation then, sir, in connection with this. As I understand it, this section did not appear in the previous act at all, and therefore it is an additional responsibility or liability of members of the armed forces. My concern is this. Certainly numerous situations arise in the armed forces which ordinarily may not arise in civilian life.
This section talks about an intention in common to carry out an unlawful purpose. In some sections of Europe to ask for a drink between eight and ten o'clock may be a breach of some code. Under these circumstances it would be most unfortunate if a group of Canadian soldiers were involved in some type of a dispute, many of whom had no thought of being involved in anything serious at all, and wound up being charged with a very serious offence because of the meaning of this section. I should like to feel that there was no question but that unlawful purpose was designated entirely within the realm of our own law and not by any definition of an outside jurisdiction.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Under the NATO arrangement, of course, we have usually the first opportunity to deal with those cases: otherwise the civil courts can deal with them under the amendments to the act which have already been brought into the house. As I understand it, so long as we apply the Canadian law that would cover unlawful purpose or any other subsidiary matter. Because we have generally the first right to try people in foreign countries for transgressing their law, it becomes a question, I should think, of relying on the judgment of the commanding officer or whoever is in charge of the unit or the area. If he failed to apply Canadian law then, in the second instance, such people can be tried under the law of the place where they are, but I cannot imagine any practical situation in relation to our own people, in any serious case, where a Canadian officer charged with the jurisdiction would pass it over to someone else.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
I am thinking of the places where the minister has indicated that by statute there has been an application of the law of the foreign jurisdiction. Notwithstanding the fact that the commanding officer, or whoever is going to be in charge of a court martial, may have the first opportunity to try an accused, would I not be right in saying that under whatever conflict of law exists he might have to apply the law of the civilian jurisdiction which has been made applicable by a previous statute or regulation to our own armed forces? If that be the case, even

Canadian Forces Act
though he might have jurisdiction to try, he might be working under a definition in those areas which would create considerable disability on the part of defence counsel.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: It would appear in the case the hon. member has mentioned that the Canadian officer or tribunal having jurisdiction would apply, under all the existing regulations and the act, the Canadian law in determining any of these matters. But if there were no Canadian law-if it happened to be an act not made an offence by Canadian law-I would think he would have to apply the law of the place where he was at the time because if he did not the foreign court could then step in and apply itr.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 8-Parties to an offence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Clause 8 obviously provides penalties for what might be called an extension of looting or the searching of and stealing from bodies of the fallen. I was wondering whether the words "in the course of warlike operations" were not a rather strict limiting factor. Suppose circumstances occurred during extensive training periods where you might perhaps find an R.C.A.F. plane had crashed and the bodies might possibly be then tampered with. Would they be covered by that clause, or does this clause only refer to the strict interpretation of the words "in the course of warlike operations"?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in most cases, of course, the ordinary law of theft would apply. It was felt however that the same amendment as was made to the army act of the United Kingdom last year after a good deal of investigation should be adopted. These particular offences which have to do with activities in the field are of a more serious nature and should be more stringently dealt with than ordinary cases of theft. I think that would also be why in subclause (g)- and this incidentally is taken directly from the British army act-the words "in the course of warlike operations" were added.
The net result of the clause which we have adopted from the British army act is that it has increased the maximum penalty. That is about the only real change; the reason being, as I have said, that it is felt that this type of offence is more heinous, more serious in the midst of activities in the field than ordinary theft.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
I can see it being classed as ordinary theft here in Canada, but let us suppose our troops in Europe were engaged in extensive activities, as they have been in recent years, and there was an unfortunate accident there and a case occurred where, to

take subclause (g) as an illustration, an attempt was made to steal from some of the men who had become unfortunate casualties. Would they be covered by this subclause or not?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: The point the hon. member has raised would not come under subclause (g). It would be a case of theft, for which the penalties are also stringent but not as stringent as they would be in this case.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: That is why I said I thought perhaps this was a rather strict limitation, and I wondered if you had considered expanding it?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: I was wondering if the minister would give us a little more explanation as to why this amendment is introduced now. It is all very well to say it is similar to section 30 of the army act, 1955, of the United Kingdom, but what has brought about the need for this to be introduced here in so far as the Canadian forces are concerned? We are not now engaged in warlike operations. Have we had anything like this in the past? Something must have brought this to a head.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, these subclauses of course do not apply in Canada at the moment. I think the reason they were introduced is because the investigation that took place in Great Britain and the changes made in their act-we try to keep in touch with the changes to the relevant acts in the United Kingdom and United States as well- commended themselves to us as being useful sections in the event of war and as being of assistance under such circumstances. There is no application at the present time, of course.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: It is aimed at looting, is it? Were the investigations carried on in Britain as a result of looting in the second world war, or were they the result of something which happened in Korea or Malaya?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
There are probably a number of reasons but I think one of the reasons is that frequently plans, documents and identification and so on which might have proved useful were removed and thrown away or scattered about. The fact that such actions have been made serious offences might tend to correct some of that sort of thing. Also in time of war I should say one has to be pretty stringent in regard to the punishment of anything savouring of theft.
The only difference in the application of these subclauses would be that the maximum penalty for stealing would be increased under the code of service discipline from 7 years, or 14 years, under certain circumstances. Incidentally, these penalties are somewhat less than those imposed under the Criminal Code.

It is a question really of making the punishment fit what they regard as the crime, I suppose. It is not a change in the definition of what constitutes theft or what constitutes an offence, but it is making optional the gradation of the seriousness of punishment.
It has also just been pointed out to me that while it is generally true that these three subclauses deal with theft, some of the offences listed here would not be strictly theft at all, but are peculiar to the warlike conditions under which we would be operating.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, but does not section 68 deal with property of the government and matters pertaining to that? Yet this amendment, certainly in subclause (i), extends to property abandoned by the enemy. The present section 68 does not go quite that far at all; it has nothing to do with enemy property.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Well, property abandoned by the enemy of course automatically becomes the property of the government of the successful country engaged. It does not lapse; it becomes the property of that country immediately.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
I would like to ask the
minister a question with respect to subclause (g), which reads:
Steals from, or with intent to steal searches, the person of any person killed or wounded, in the course of warlike operations:
I remember at Ypres we were advancing on one occasion. We had been in the trenches for a week or two and my feet swelled up so I could hardly bear my boots. When we were advancing I ran across a poor unfortunate Australian, and I stopped for a few minutes and took off his boots and put them on. Would a soldier be guilty of an offence under this clause under those circumstances?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: I would not think he would under the circumstances outlined by the hon. member.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: I suppose it would be a question, as the deputy minister of justice says, of being morally innocent.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: I remember in the first war we were quite short of equipment, and it was a common practice to take a pair of binoculars or a revolver from a German officer and use it for our own personal use. We did not call it stealing, we called it commandeering. Would a man doing those things be liable under this clause?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
In the last war you just gave them a receipt signed "Joe Blow".
Canadian Forces Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
I think this matter deserves a little more consideration. As has just been mentioned, enemy property taken during the first war was considered to be commandeered, whereas in the second world war it was considered to be liberated. I think a little haste has been shown in inserting this particular amendment without giving full consideration to all the possibilities. A good example was given by the hon. member for Kootenay West. Anyone who served overseas can recall multiple instances of these things; and while the minister may say that under those circumstances an officer or man would not be charged, I am not too sure. If we had a particularly efficient adjutant general's department and a very efficient provost corps, troops who were doing commandeering or liberating at the front might be borne down upon quite heavily. I would not want to give the adjutant general or the provost corps any more power than they have at the present time.
I fail to understand why this amendment should be suddenly brought forward during peacetime. In case of war it might be necessary to be more careful with regard to looting, although section 68 of the National Defence Act seems to provide sufficient protection against this offence. I think it goes far enough. If we write into the National Defence Act something which cannot be enforced, then we will be bringing the law into disrepute. I do not see how you could enforce this clause in the field under actual service conditions. There would be enemy property that was abandoned, and it would be taken otherwise than for the public service. I can assure you of that. If a person were on the stand he might be able to declare that what he had done with the abandoned enemy property was for the public service, but he would be in an awkward position.
If this section concerned only our own people or our allies from whom things were taken, that would be a different matter entirely; but when it comes to the enemy I am not at all sure that you can effectively guard against what appear to people in the field to be legitimate operations. I suggest to the minister that he withhold this particular amendment for further consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
This clause has been brought forward because the people in the department agree with the British that we should profit from some of the experiences of the past and get our statute in shape to deal with emergencies that might occur, although we hope they will not occur. It seems to me

Canadian Forces Act
that any provisions which might tend to discourage the wrongs that might occur in warlike operations, particularly anything savouring of looting or of dealing carelessly with valuable documents and so on, would be of extreme value. Such provisions would prove to be most beneficial if war should break out.
The subsections do not apply in peacetime, but if unfortunately we should be involved in a war I think we should be able to deal with these matters very stringently. Probably in a new war we would have to deal with them more stringently than was the case in any past war.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
I still am not convinced that we have to introduce this section. British experience may point to the need of it, but Canadian experience has been rather extensive. I gather from the minister's remarks that the request for this has emerged from the intelligence branch. I imagine they have felt that some valuable material was lost in the last war, or perhaps in Korea, which would have been most useful to their service. Of course a good point can be made on the basis of the requirements of intelligence, but I still am far from being convinced that we need to write this into the act at the present time. I do not know that the minister has advanced sufficient reasons for it being incorporated in the act when section 68 has served so well up to the present.
I do not object to the department looking at what is being done in the United Kingdom or the United States with regard to matters of this sort, but we have a very extensive Canadian experience in service problems, and if this has not been brought up by Canadian service personnel as the result of Canadian experience in active theatres of war I think it might well be held over.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: I think the word "steal" should be defined. A man who takes for his own use and does it out in the open with everybody knowing about it is not stealing, but a man who takes in order to sell so that he may put money in his own pocket is really stealing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: What about the man who holds up a bank?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: I think the last suggestion is worthy of consideration. The word "stealing" should be defined. I remember losing my compass in France and I was lost without it. I found another, and made use of it. Was that stealing? It was not mine, but it helped me out of a difficulty.

Clause agreed to.

On clause 9-Improper driving of vehicles.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Dealing with paragraph (c), the minister will be aware that certain drugs are used in the treatment of illness which are capable of impairing the ability to drive a motor vehicle. It seems to me it would be unfortunate if the penalty provided by this clause were to be applied in such cases. I think some exception should be made in paragraph (c) to cover drugs which are used under a prescription by a medical officer.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext: Surely if a man is impaired by the use of a drug he should not be driving a vehicle, even though the drug has been administered for medical purposes. The person certainly would be aware that he had been treated with such a drug, and whether his driving capacity had been impaired to the danger of the public and other motorists on the highway. Surely the test must be whether, by reason of alcohol or by the use of a drug, under any circumstances he has become a danger or a menace on the highway.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
Subparagraph (c) states: having charge of a vehicle of the Canadian forces knowingly permits it to be driven by a person whose ability to drive such a vehicle is impaired by alcohol or a drug; is guilty of an offence . . .
Private soldiers are placed in charge of vehicles. If the private soldier has that vehicle taken by an intoxicated superior officer, whether he is a corporal, a sergeant, a sergeant major or a commissioned officer, who bears the blame? It is the private soldier against whom the vehicle is charged. Would he bear the penalty, or what would the army do under those circumstances?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
Generally speaking, the
senior officer in the vehicle is in charge of the vehicle, and this amendment is intended to make that very clear. He should not be in that condition, and the intention of this subclause is to make the officer in the vehicle responsible for the driving, whoever under him is actually driving it. I think it is only fair and proper that he should be.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
I think the minister has missed the point of the question by the hon. member. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT

speechtext: As a hypothetical question, supposing there is a sergeant in charge of the vehicle and an officer comes down insisting on a vehicle, what happens then?

speechtext:

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT
speechtext:
Then in this' particular case, if I might pursue it, reading subclause 2, it has even removed one of the possible defences available to the accused
Canadian Forces Act
under the Criminal Code. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fulton for the second reading of Bill No. 52, to amend the Income Tax Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ASSESSMENTS, BOOKS AND RECORDS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate was adjourned on April 24 by the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White). Does he intend to continue?
I wish to make a few remarks with reference to the argument put up by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and the hon. member for Middlesex East. In the debate the hon. member for Kamloops dealt at some length with the principles which he considered were involved. However, the argument of the hon. member for Middlesex East was mostly along the line of particular cases. I think the particular cases could, with all reasonableness, be dealt with when the estimates of the department come before the house. I may say that the estimates of the Department of National Revenue, taxation

division, have already been before the select committee, and most of the principles and a lot of the details were dealt with in that committee. If those who are interested would follow the report of the proceedings that took place there probably they could get answers to most of the questions of the type that had been raised both when this bill was before the house and by hon. members on different occasions.
What I want to say is there can be no doubt at all that it is highly desirable-and the department agrees with this-that every taxpayer in the country should be able to settle and determine with finality the amount of his liability for income tax as quickly as it is practically possible. The government has accepted in principle the idea that there should be a point beyond which the crown cannot go back and change an assessment unless the taxpayer was guilty of fraud or misrepresentation. With this in mind, the six-year limitation was introduced in the income tax in 1944. Since that time progress has been made in getting the work of the taxation division more up to date and the Minister of Finance, who perhaps may have something to say in the course of this debate, has considered the possibility of shortening the six-year term; that is under consideration. Whether the three-year limit proposed in this bill is suitable or not, it is not a limitation that we can accept at this time until further studies have been made.
Mention has been made here of the fact that very considerable progress has been made in getting the work of the taxation division up to date. Ten years ago, or 12 years ago, from 1945 on, there was a great backlog of work which had to be done. That backlog was the accumulation of unassessed returns, because of the fact that during the war years a great number of our staff had been diverted into private enterprise and it became increasingly hard to recruit people to do the work. At that time I remember we had somewhere between 11,000 and 12,000 employees in the central office here, in what we call the head office, and in the 28 divisions which we have throughout the country. I am very happy to say that that backlog of work has been cleaned up and we are now on a current basis. The same amount of work, or considerably more work, is now being done with 6,000 to 7,000 employees that was formerly done by 11,000 or more.
From the consideration of the precise period of time, three years, which has been suggested, I should like to turn briefly to the technical aspects of the bill. The bill recognizes the possibility of conflict with section
Income Tax Act
42 of the act. Section 42 has to do with assessments averaging for farmers and fishermen. Therefore, if the investigation were only a three-year period there would be a conflict in that averaging which is given to farmers and fishermen.
It should be noted that section 43 operates in much the same way as section 42. It is immediately apparent that the operation of sections 53, 64 and 80 might be seriously affected. Further study will no doubt reveal other provisions that would require some changes. This is not the kind of thing we should rush into without first deciding what to do about those other provisions, some of which have been inserted for alleviation of the tax burden.
Let me deal with the technical aspects of the bill. I suggest it does not say what the hon. member for Kamloops has in mind. In line 18 we find the words:
Such assessment shall be deemed to be final.
In lines 21 and 22 we find the words:
Such assessment shall not thereafter be subject to be re-opened or varied.
The words "such assessments" refer back only to the original assessment mentioned earlier in the section. No account is taken of the possibility that there may already have been a subsequent assessment that varied the original assessment. Furthermore, this language is much stronger than that found in section 46, and it appears to be in conflict with subsection 7 of that section, which provides for the assessment being varied as the result of an objection or an appeal.
I feel sure the sponsor of this bill did not intend that court decisions must be reached within three years. I only point this out as one of the technical oversights that makes the bill somewhat objectionable. More serious objection to be found with the substance of the bill is the manner in which it would hamper investigation. As I read it, it specifically provides that the taxation division cannot investigate returns more than three years old unless fraud is alleged in respect of that particular year. To allege fraud or wilful misrepresentation is a very serious matter. It is not something that can be done before investigation starts. Though the officials investigating might have very good reason for thinking some income has been omitted from a taxpayer's return, or that income has been incorrectly calculated, or even though they may suspect fraud, I assure the house it is not their practice to allege fraud before seeking substantial corroborative evidence. Even where fraud has been proven in a current year I would hesitate to ask anyone to allege fraud in a previous year

Income Tax Act
before it had been possible to investigate those previous years. Yet this is what the bill appears to require.
Early in 1955 a case was completed in a certain city in Canada involving a group of individuals and corporations engaged in a certain type of business. The corporations and the individuals were convicted of evading more than $600,000 of taxes, with charges laid for each of the years 1942 to 1952. This investigation was started in 1952. Careful and thorough planning was necessary to ensure that evidence would be available. This was particularly true because immediately prior to starting the investigation reassessments involving additional taxes of only a few hundred dollars were made, based on the books and records made available by the corporations and the individuals concerned. Does the house wish to circumscribe and hinder investigations which have produced and will continue to produce such results?
I do not think this matter of investigation should be left without pointing out to the house that in fraud cases much of the information is obtained from sources other than the taxpayer's own books and records. The right to inquire from or require information from persons applies to "any person" and not just the person being investigated. The proposed bill would make it impossible to get information, in many cases, from suppliers, customers and banks without advising those parties that the department has alleged fraud. It is bad enough, indeed, to tell the taxpayer at an early stage of the investigation that the department is alleging fraud, but surely it is highly undesirable, to say the least, to insert provisions that would spread the knowledge that the department has alleged fraud or wilful misrepresentation to many of the taxpayer's business associates. His name would be blackened before the matter was brought before the courts.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that the author of this bill had any intention of giving any protection or assistance to anyone who is deliberately evading taxes. I am quite sure that he had not. However, I feel sure that after close scrutiny of the provisions before us the house will agree that something more than the words before us is necessary and that we should take a cautious approach to this subject.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat I am not averse to a further limitation of the powers to reassess, having regard to all the considerations this house had when the present six-year limitation was introduced, and I may say the matter was considered before the present income tax bill was brought down. To my knowledge, however, the change has not been

made but I am going to let the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) give the reasons for that. The ramifications of the effects of this bill, in some cases adverse to taxpayers, have not been fully studied in its drafting. I accordingly must oppose the bill at this time in its present form.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ASSESSMENTS, BOOKS AND RECORDS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to be very brief indeed; I have not the capacity this afternoon to talk for more than about three minutes.
We commend the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) for his diligence and attention to this problem. I am quite sure he has brought it forward because he realizes it is a matter of serious concern to a large number of Canadians. Hon. members in this group have received similar complaints and have had similar suggestions made for some amendment to the present form of assessment going back for a number of years.
While we feel the bill would possibly not achieve all the hon. member aims to achieve at this time-and I listened with great interest to the minister's remarks-and although possibly it has some minor defects, nevertheless we in this group intend to support the bill, Mr. Speaker. We give our support to the purpose of the hon. member for Kamloops in bringing this matter before the house and introducing this bill. That purpose is one we heartily agree with. It is to provide justice for all Canadian taxpayers and a system of income tax administration that will receive the unqualified support of the majority of fair-minded citizens.

speechtext:
We must consider what in fact is justice to the taxpayers of Canada. I am not going to argue anything at all except this. The payment of taxes is the greatest form of justice that can be exercised to the taxpayers of Canada. A government must be in a position to collect taxes equally and fairly from those who should pay them. It may very well happen that with a staff which, while not limited in numbers, nevertheless is not

increased particularly at any given time, that a government collecting agency would fall behind in normal work in collecting taxes. It also means that the person who inadvertently, as well as the person who deliberately, avoids the payment of taxes may not possibly be reached in the ordinary way without the passage of some time.
I think we all agree on this, that if we are going to exempt people from taxation because they have not been assessed by a particular period of time, it must be on the assumption that first of all we can afford not to have those taxes and secondly that we should place in the hands of the government every facility to have assessed that person and collected the taxes by that particular time.
Now, that is the issue at this particular moment. My hon. friend says he wants to limit the amount of time within which the government can collect taxes, except on certain conditions, from the Canadian taxpayers as a whole. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) has indicated that in the normal course of events it is likely that people will not be assessed until a certain time has elapsed. I am in the position as the Minister of Finance of having to say to my colleague that if that is the case it will be necessary then for me to give that department at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer additional people, additional inspectors, additional assessors, in order that we can be sure the three or four million people who pay taxes in this country can in fact be assessed within a given time.
Now then, in addition to that, we are going to say to the Minister of National Revenue that if in the course of his investigations he finds that Mr. A has not paid his taxes when he should have and if he finds this perchance by some other means-not by just going to his house-he is not entitled to use that information if a certain time has run by unless, as I understand the bill, he can prove that the individual deliberately and fraudulently avoided the payment of taxes.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, there is bound to be a period of time after which you will not do this. We have always thought the six years was a reasonable length of time. As far as I am concerned, I quite understand the vexation that may be attendant upon a person who thinks he has and who has in fact settled his accounts and then finds at a later time that he has not. On the other hand, I am conscious of the fact that six years is not in my view too long generally for this kind of work to be done under present circumstances and that if you abridge
Income Tax Act
the time-at least if you abridge it as substantially as the present bill suggests-you are undoubtedly going to place the government of Canada in a position-I am not going to say of doubling the number of people employed for this purpose-of substantially increasing it or of asking me to admit in the house that it will be impossible to collect all the taxes that ought to be paid by citizens who want to pay their taxes and those who try to avoid so doing.
Under those circumstances, sir, we gave consideration last year-I might say before the budget was presented-to this problem and we gave consideration to it again this year and we could not come to the conclusion that we should abridge the time at the present moment without the possibility that we would be deprived of a considerable sum of money which we think we are entitled to in fairness to all the Canadian taxpayers who are paying their taxes. It may be possible that the time could be abridged less than what the hon. member for Kamloops has in mind. 1 quite agree that we would remove some of the vexatious difficulties if we did that, but I am not satisfied yet, and I accept the responsibility for the decision, not my colleague the Minister of National Revenue, that at this moment we cannot accept the bill. All I can say is that we have made progress in the two discussions we have had last year and this year in examining the whole problem to see if we could not cut down the six years. Therefore in the meantime I propose to oppose the bill for that reason, and that reason alone.

The minister has modified somewhat my impression of what he said earlier, but I think it will be found on Hansard that he did say something very much to the effect that he was not prepared as yet to admit that six years was too long, that in fact it could be reduced below six years. It seems to me that the only thing to do is to call for a decision on the bill and the principle involved in the bill.
The principle involved in the bill is that there should be a limitation of three years after the date of a final assessment within

which the department must reopen an assessment unless it alleges fraud or wilful misrepresentation, and that after a three-year period from the date of the final assessment the assessment will become not subject to reopening or review unless, as I say, there is then an allegation of fraud or wilful misrepresentation.
The Minister of National Revenue said that there was some possible conflict with sections 43, 53, 64 and 80 of the act. I do not pretend to be an expert draftsman but in the short time available to me I have looked at the act and I cannot see that there is any irreconcilable conflict. I believe that by and large those sections have to do with averaging and they would prevail if there were no conflict. The bill expressly preserves the right of averaging given in section 42 and therefore I cannot see that there would be any conflict which would work to the detriment of the taxpayer as between the new clauses set out in this bill and the sections of the act mentioned by the minister.
I was interested in his criticism of the proposed amendment. The minister referred to the words in paragraph (b) (i) as follows:
Such assessment shall not thereafter be subject to be re-opened or varied.
The bill does not take account of the possibility of a reassessment having been made after the first assessment but within a three-year period. I would refer the minister to the provisions of subclause (b) of the proposed new clause 4, which reads:
After the expiry of 3 years from the day of the original assessment, and subject only to the provisions of subparagraph (i) of paragraph (a) of this subsection,-
Subparagraph (i) of paragraph (a) gives the minister the right to insist on an investigation in the event of wilful misrepresentation or fraud at any time after three years, notwithstanding whether reassessments have been made or not. That situation is protected by the use of the words "subject only to the provisions of subparagraph (i) of paragraph (a)".
Then the minister said that the language with respect to the final nature of the assessment was stronger than the language of the present section 46 in that it would now be necessary for the department to allege fraud or wilful misrepresentation if it wanted to reopen after three years. That result does follow from the language of my bill and it is a result which I deliberately sought to accomplish in wording the bill. Let me point out in answer to the many objections raised by the two ministers that if the three-year limit from the original assessment was adapted it would still give the department virtually four years to carry out its investigations.

The original assessment, whilst it is provided in section 46 that it must be made with all due dispatch, is nevertheless not made usually for some months and in some cases going on for a year after the filing of the return. By the proposed bill there is a further three-year period from that time, within which they may carry on investigations, so that in effect they are given from 3| to 4 years to carry on investigations and make reassessments if there is found to be any irregularity. That should be, in my submission, ample time, so that one is justified in providing that, after that time has expired, then the assessment can be reopened or varied only if the department is prepared to allege fraud or deliberate misrepresentation.
In my view, as I said in introducing the bill, and I repeat now, I am not seeking to protect the dishonest or fraudulent taxpayer. The necessity of the allegation of fraud or misrepresentation after there has been plenty of time to make an investigation, that is, 3i to 4 years, would have a rather wholesome effect in that it would discourage the making of investigations which in many instances at the present time smack almost of persecution. I know it would be a serious allegation and I think it would give the department second thought before it instituted an investigation if it had to allege fraud or misrepresentation. I am not at all uncertain-in fact I am satisfied-that that would not be an unhealthy situation, because on the basis of the evidence now available it is our view that there are too many investigations too carelessly undertaken after the lapse of six or seven years, when the taxpayer has no possibility of producing the evidence that is required and, simply because he cannot prove his innocence, all the cards are in the hands of the department, and the innocent taxpayer is presumed to be guilty.
Sir, it is to correct that situation that I introduce the bill. Nothing said by the two ministers this afternoon has led me to believe that the principle should not be accepted, and I therefore recommend it for the verdict of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take long tonight in connection with the second reading of this bill since I spoke only yesterday at the resolution stage. I think however I might refer again to the fact that this bill, which provides for the money to be available for the Canadian National Railways for capital expenditures during the current year, and also covers a sufficient amount to take care of the same type of expenditure for Trans-Canada Airlines, is the usual type of bill. But at the

same time it seems to me we might seriously devote a little more attention to the problem of the railway's financing, because if we do not look at these expenditures as we go along it may be possible the formula which was put into effect in 1952 covering the capital outstanding at that time might again be placed in jeopardy.
The president of the railway was very fair in giving the sessional committee on railways and shipping the benefit of his experience in connection with these financing problems. I think it is well to remember that Mr. Gordon is a man with a vast banking and financial background. I think he has brought to the railway that wide experience, and we should pay considerable attention to what he says in connection with the financial position of the railway.
I would like to read to you, if I may, some of Mr. Gordon's words as reported at page 261 of the minutes of the committee dealing with the very crucial problem concerning the ability of the railway to continue to carry the carrying charges on the outstanding capital and at the same time to meet its operating expenses. This is what Mr. Gordon said:
But two questions have to be met. One is that this apparently satisfactory result has been due in large measure to the high returns which we obtained from our capital expenditure on the dieselization program. In the early stages of dieselization those savings were at their maximum because we deliberately selected those services which would give us the biggest return. We have now entered upon the stage where though the whole program is still based on economic considerations the amount of return will be subject to the law of diminishing returns. I can say therefore that we are just at the point of having to worry about our ability to keep ourselves in that position, and one of the most difficult problems confronting the Canadian National management is to ensure that the economic benefits which are scheduled to accrue in connection with this capital expenditure-
I might say that is the capital expenditure we are talking about voting here tonight.
-are not diverted into meeting steadily increasing current costs, the most important of which are wages and materials. If we find that the savings which we get from these capital expenditures have to be used to meet rising current costs they will not be available to prove the point I am making. If we cannot increase current revenues and get them adjusted to offset the effect of current cost increases the net result would be a growing inability to provide any return whatever on our equity investment and make it increasingly difficult to service the outstanding debt out of our earnings.
And then on the next page, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Gordon referred to the fact that the amount of money which was being spent was on expenditures which he deemed prudent.
