This is getting back to the position I discussed very briefly yesterday. Capital expenditures themselves require a certain fixed sum to be made annually by the railway to meet the carrying charges on the same. The president of the railway has said that these are prudent expenditures. The expenditure of these moneys will show a return sufficient to carry the outlay made, but if the railway finds itself in the position, in connection with its current operations, where it has to cut down to the point where it cannot make sufficient money to take care of that fixed amount, then of course we are going to find ourselves back in the same position we were in several years ago when the government had to put up the money to meet the carrying charges on the guaranteed bonds.
I suggest, sir, that perhaps we have to take a different outlook in this connection. Perhaps we will have to arrive at a new formula. If these expenditures are prudent, as the management of the railway believes they are, then there is a fixed amount which must be set aside as the amount which must be earned annually out of those prudent expenditures to take care of the carrying charges on them.
If it is apparent in the other half of the formula that the current revenues are not in a position to do that job and meet the current operating expenses, then I think we have reached a stage where the railway must be given more freedom in order to carry out its operations. It must not be left in the position where it is always between the squeeze on the one hand of keeping certain of its expenditures down, the squeeze of keeping its charges down, and at the other extreme facing the annual demand for increasing wages.
As I said previously, I do not think labour is very happy with this situation because they feel there has been placed on top of the whole operation a blanket type of control, and when they move into negotiations they are not moving into unfettered negotiations and there is a ceiling put on their aspirations. They are not going to be happy, I believe, until they see management in a position to meet their legitimate demands and at the same time plot the course for the railway

Canadian National Railways without a continual reference year after year to a board of some kind to see exactly where they stand.
I am not suggesting tonight the board has to be removed. I simply say that we should be plotting a course to put in management's hands more of the ability to meet every-day competition and to plot its own future without being hamstrung at every turn.
In connection with this situation I think it is advisable for us to move along that line in any case. It seems to me, once we have determined that there should be an operation of a company by the public and once we have provided for the public corporation to do the job, it is our duty to see that the company has the tools with which to carry out the job.
I think one of the things we should be making a point of is that we do not snipe continually year after year at some type of operation such as this. We should give them the tools to do the job and as long as they are not coming back and calling on us to meet recurring types of operating deficits- they have some excuse if they do not have the freedom they need-but as long as they are not doing that, I do not think we should be bothering them at every turn in connection with their policies.
In connection with this legislation I notice that Trans-Canada Air Lines is mentioned. It seems to me that we are moving to the point where even with government corporations there can be a conflict of interests and I submit that these two corporations should be separated. As far as I can see there seems to be no particular reason why the capital expenditures of Trans-Canada Air Lines should be intermingled with legislation dealing with Canadian National Railways.
As a matter of fact, I am a little confused as to who is responsible for this type of legislation. I notice that questions having to do with Canadian National Railways are answered by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), but when legislation deals with the financing of Canadian National Railways it is handled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), and then when Trans-Canada Air Lines enters the picture the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) squeezes in. There is certainly confusion in connection with this type of legislation and I think it is time that the two corporations should be separated before a real conflict of interests arises.
I might suggest also that it is about time the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has a big pipe-line job on his hands, should divest himself of T.C.A. and let it come back where it should be, to the Minister of Transport. The minister has several jobs and it

There is something about the form of this bill which reminds me of the other bill we had this afternoon; that is, it combines subject matters which for many years were dealt with in two separate bills. I must not break the rule by referring to the clauses but there is no law against Your Honour looking at the bill which you have in your hand and noticing that the last clause deals with a subject matter which for many years was covered by a completely separate bill.
As I say, this afternoon we had a bill which amended two different acts of the parliament of Canada. I wonder sometimes just how far this practice can be carried. I recognize that it is much more convenient for the government to reduce the number of bills it has to bring before parliament. If it could go on combining bills into one it might do something about the length of the session and something about the problems which this government has in facing parliament.
Canadian National Railways
Frankly I see no reason why the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) should be allowed to put all of his bills for the session into one bill; I see no reason why the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) should be permitted to put in one bill what used to be in one bill introduced by the Minister of Finance and in another bill introduced by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), unless the same privilege is to be extended to the other ministers. I certainly hope it will not be done, for I checked and discovered that so far this session the Minister of Transport has presented five different bills, the Minister of Finance has presented six or seven different bills, the Minister of Public Works has given us three, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce has given us at least three bills. So I might go on with the rest of the ministers.
The excuse given this afternoon by the Minister of National Defence was that it was a matter of convenience to have all the national defence legislation for a year in one bill. I am sure, too, it is a matter of convenience to the Minister of Finance to be able to do this, but I suggest that if that can be done there is nothing to stop each minister in the cabinet from putting all his legislation for the year into one bill and saying, "This is my department's legislation for the year." Maybe it is carrying it to the point of absurdity, but we have seen this government do absurd things, to say that after a few years of that kind of practice the Prime Minister might bring before us one bill containing all the legislation for the session.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I have little to add at this time to what I said at the resolution stage. The gold mining industry continues to face difficult economic problems. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very brief bill. It purports to add the word and figures "1957 and 1958" to the provisions of one of the clauses of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. This measure has been in effect now for eight years. The subsidy has been offered since 1948. In that period of time there have been various debates on measures to

extend the effect of the subsidy. In each case the measure has been supported by the house, and no new principle is involved in the present bill.
I think a word should be said on the matter of subsidies. I think that any subsidy requires some justification in normal times. There are dangers in subsidies. There are particular dangers in hidden subsidies. The subsidy we are dealing with here is not a hidden subsidy. This subsidy has been, from the outset, nothing more than a stop-gap, hand-to-mouth form of emergency assistance to the gold mining industry. It has never been a solution of the problems of that industry. When I say "hand-to-mouth", I am stressing particularly the fact that the measure has never been in effect at any one time for more than a couple of years. Hence the industry has not known very far in advance how long it could expect to receive this form of assistance.
There are justifications for this particular subsidy, far as it falls short of being anything like a solution of the problems of the industry. There are several grounds upon which, for lack of a proper solution, the subsidy can be justified. First of all, this is one commodity on which government sets the price. I do not say that the Canadian government has the absolute control of the setting of the price. Nevertheless, it is a commodity the price of which is definitely determined by government. In that respect it differs from almost any other commodity that is produced in Canada.
In the second place, there can be no question as to the need of the industry for some form of assistance in the absence of a proper solution of the whole problem. The plight of the gold mining industry in Canada is serious, as it has been for some years. It has been ground between the upper and nether millstones, the upper one being the set price, a ceiling on the price realized from the product, and the nether stone being the rising cost of production. Indeed, as the Canadian dollar has strengthened in terms of international exchange the position of the Canadian gold producers has deteriorated correspondingly.
It is not simply a matter, though, of the need of the industry as a producer of wealth. We are obliged to look more widely at the plight of those communities which are dependent on the gold mining industry, and there are many of them in Canada. The growth and prosperity of such communities on the one hand or their atrophy and depression on the other depend in effect on whether the ore bodies in the adjacent mines are to be operated and worked at a profit or not.
12, 1956	4971
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act When the margins are so narrow as they have been in the gold mining industry, a very slight difference in price can mean the difference between value for an ore body and literally no value at all in terms of workability.
The plight of the industry is not the fault of the industry. I do not think anyone in this house is going to question the fact that the industry has done its best, in the face of the difficulties that have confronted it, to keep itself on an efficient basis. The recent report of the Knox committee in Ontario as well as things that have been said in this house bear testimony to the fact that the industry has not been lacking in energy, enterprise and the desire to maintain all possible efficiency in production.
I have mentioned two factors, Mr. Speaker, that lend justification to the provision of a subsidy with respect to gold:	The fact that
the price is established by governments, and second, that the industry needs some form of assistance, otherwise it is going to close down further.
The third of these factors is the national interest. To an extent that some Canadians unhappily have forgotten, the gold mining industry in Canada has been one of the most effective contributing factors to the health of the Canadian economy. The search for gold has been an impelling factor in the development of great areas of Canada, not confined alone now to the extraction of gold but of other metals as well, both precious and base. In the depression years the gold mining industry stood out like a beacon light in the Canadian economy. Indeed, the prosperity of that industry in the days of the depression went far to sustain a weakened economy in Canada. In the war years the industry played a leading part, particularly in the early years of the war, again in the strengthening of the Canadian economy; and who can say that the day may not come when we shall again need the strengthening quality of the gold mining industry to help to lend support to the rest of the Canadian economy?
At any rate, this industry has an assured market for its product. It has an assured market for its product in the country where we most wish at the present time to sell some of our products. I refer to the United States. With that country in our commodity trade we are incurring a huge trading deficit. In 1955 that commodity trading deficit with the United States amounted to close to $1 billion, and in the first four months of this year it is evident that that commodity trading deficit with the United States is increasing. We have these figures from the dominion bureau of statistics. For the first four months of this
4972	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act year, 1956, our imports from the United States amounted to $1,363 million. Our exports to the United States amounted to $860 million. Therefore, in these first four months of the present fiscal year, Mr. Speaker, we have incurred a deficit of $500 million on our commodity trading account with the United States.
In the face of that situation and particularly having regard to the historical strength of the gold mining industry and what it has meant to the health of the Canadian economy, I submit to this house that it would be extremely dangerous to the Canadian economy if we contemplated a serious decline in the gold mining industry. Apart from a few mines which are blessed with very high-grade ore, the fact is undeniable that without some form of assistance, lacking an adequate solution to the problem, mines will be closed and the industry will suffer a body blow under present conditions. There are also many communities in this country directly dependent upon the gold mining industry which would atrophy and decay.
We may remind ourselves that already the process of decay in the gold mining industry has gone far, even with the very limited form of assistance that has been available to the industry under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. There are today in operation only half of the producers that were in operation in the year 1941, which is just 15 years ago. Had growth been normal there would have been many additional mines added to the group of Canadian producers. Development work has been curtailed. No one is seeking to open up new gold mines today and half of those mines that were producing in 1941 have closed down in these intervening 15 years.
It is fair also, Mr. Speaker, that we should ask what this form of assistance has cost the treasury of this country. In the eight years that it has been in effect it has cost the treasury $90 million. The extent of this aid was greatly reduced in 1955 as compared with the previous year, 1954. That year, 1954, was the record in terms of assistance advanced to the gold mining industry, when $16-3 million was paid out of the treasury of this country to the industry under the terms of this legislation. In 1955 the total of assistance under the revised formula that was introduced at the time the legislation was before this house last was just $9-3 million, and it is estimated that if this measure is continued in effect for the remainder of 1956 and the years 1957 and 1958, as proposed in the present measure, the assistance in this year, 1956, will cost the public treasury $8-9 million, and in the year 1957, $8-6 million. The


scale of assistance under the revised formula is moving steadily downward.
The purpose of this bill, sir, is to extend the effect of the legislation for two years. It is right and proper that this measure to extend the provisions of the act should be introduced now rather than that the industry should be left in doubt until the legislation would otherwise expire at the end of 1956. It is right and proper that it should be introduced now. Indeed, if it had been left until later, serious injury would be done to the industry because the mines must know in time to make their plans. Had it been the intention of the government to let this form of assistance expire at the end of 1956, or had the industry been left in doubt as to the plans of this government or as to the intention of the government with respect to it, then the plight of the industry would have been very serious, indeed.
I have emphasized, sir, that this measure is no solution of the deep-seated problem of the gold mining industry. The difficulty and the flaw in measures of this kind is that they often lull the government and lull parliament into thinking that the problem has been solved, or at least the problem has been met for the time being. No hon. member should delude himself into thinking that this measure is any solution, even on the short-run basis, of the needs and the problems of the goldmining industry. These problems are going to require much more farsighted solutions than are offered by the hand-to-mouth, stopgap type of assistance that we have in the present measure.
The importance of gold in the world has not receded in these recent years. There is not a country in all the world that does not want more gold. The heroic measures of austerity which the British government has found it necessary to impose upon the economy of that country have been designed to retain and recapture an increased quantity out of the world's store of gold. The possession of gold is a leading factor in the fiscal and trading policy of every country in the whole world.
Last year parliament approved some easing in the restrictions that theretofore had been applied in this country with respect to the holding of gold in private hands and the coinage of gold. But, Mr. Speaker, no one I am sure is going to pretend that these were anything more than very, very slight palliatives. These were no solution. What is required is something much more far-reaching. That leads me to say just a brief word about the relationship of this country and of this government with the International Monetary Fund.

It is evident that our engagements with the International Monetary Fund are such that the government has not a free hand to pursue the goal of an increased price for newly-mined gold apart from some permission on the part of the International Monetary Fund. I have been urging for years now that the government has the responsibility to Canada and to the gold mining industry to pursue with very much greater vigour and determination the need of a higher price for newly-mined Canadian gold. That, in the last analysis, is the only solution of the problem of the gold mining industry. An upward adjustment in price is overdue.
The government has been very chary in even acquainting the house with what it may have proposed at meetings of the board of governors of the International Monetary Fund. It has been like drawing teeth to try to extract any information from them as to what they have urged. We do know that South Africa with similar interests has been pressing its case very strongly before the International Monetary Fund for an increase in the price of newly-mined gold. This country, this house and the gold mining industry of this country are entitled to know what the Canadian government is doing in the same regard, and are entitled to expect vigour and determination on the part of the government and the exercise of the utmost ingenuity at meetings of the governing body of the International Monetary Fund in seeking some solution to this problem, which is not going to be solved apart from an upward adjustment in the price of newly-mined gold.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we are entitled in this regard to ask the Canadian government for a statement of its own policy with reference to the holding of gold. What is the degree of confidence that the Canadian government is prepared to demonstrate in the future of gold-gold as a factor in our fiscal, trading and, indeed, all our economic relations? If the Canadian government wished to give some striking evidence of their belief in the future of gold to a country that is a substantial gold producer, and would be a much greater gold producer if a profitable market awaited it, it could give a striking demonstration of that confidence in the future of gold by making a bold declaration in regard to its own policy in reference to gold holdings.
In the budget papers tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) which are appended to the speech he delivered on the occasion of the introduction of his budget on March 20, we find in table 11 on page 24 the holdings of gold and of United States dollars of the exchange fund account and the Bank of Canada.

In 1952 gold holdings were $885 million; United States dollars $961-8 million. In 1953 gold holdings had increased to $986-1 million; United States dollars had decreased to $802 million. It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker, tlmt in the presence of the Minister of Finance as well as the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) I urge this is a time when the Canadian government ought to be bold in declaring a policy with regard to the holding of gold in the exchange fund account and the Bank of Canada. Having regard to the seriousness of the" plight of the gold mining industry, having; regard to the imperative necessity for finding, a solution, having regard to the fact that any subsidy measure like the present one is at: best only to be supported on the basis of ar? existing emergency, then I submit, Mr. Speaker, we must have a serious engagement on the part of the Canadian government to address itself to the problem and to bring forth a solution. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has more or less dealt with the rarefied and to me somewhat mysterious atmosphere of international finance and gold supply and so on. My remarks will be directly related to the somewhat more earthy subject of the lives of the miners and the communities in which they live.
This group has supported the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act since it was first introduced in the house as a temporary legislative palliative that maintains employment and in so doing protects the livelihood of the miners and others concerned, their investments in their homes and their investments in their communities. However, Mr. Speaker, we are not certain that the legislation is being used to the best advantage of the miners and the others concerned and of the country as a whole. We think it is about time there was some consideration given to a possible amendment to the act to make it more flexible to meet a situation which is not only temporary but which appears to be somewhat like some positions in the government service-it is a permanent-temporary situation.
Until comparatively recently all mining operations, whether base metal or gold, generally speaking followed a similar wage policy throughout Canada. While rates varied somewhat from area to area, within a given area the wages were practically identical in all types of mining. I am informed that this was particularly true in Canada's two main gold mining camps, Kirkland Lake and Porcupine. In fact I am informed that their wage policies were identical and extended into the base metal mines in northwestern Quebec. I am informed also that this solid policy or front which extended to even having the same negotiators handle their dealings with the unions was broken down about a year ago when Noranda, a base metal producer at Noranda, Quebec, granted the 44-hour week and certain wage concessions. I presume the reason for that change was the rise in the price of copper from 36 cents to 46 cents in a little more than a year and the development of the uranium mines in the Blind River area.


I understand that at that time the Ontario and Quebec mining operators were faced with a labour shortage. I am informed also that hundreds of miners left the Kirkland Lake area and the Timmins area last fall and winter for the base metal and uranium mines because of the higher wage scales and better employment advantages. As a matter of fact, regardless of the beneficial effects of the act, it has not been completely effective in preventing a lessening of the population in those two important areas.
The gold mining operators under that situation were faced with two alternatives. First, the prosperous gold mines could raise their rates to compete with the base metal and uranium mines for labour which would have provided a somewhat realistic view of the prosperity of the gold mining industry. Second, they could join together with the marginal mines and present the gold mining operators' version of a solid wage scale front on behalf of the operators concerned.
As I understand it, the gold mining operators chose a combination of these two alternatives. They introduced the 44-hour week without making any wage concessions. They thus left themselves considerably behind the base metal and uranium mines in regard to rates. Apparently they had hoped that the fact that most of their miners had an investment in their homes would force them to forgo the higher rates of pay available elsewhere in the mining industry. That was their first proposal.
The second part of their plan provided for the tapping of a labour supply willing to accept rates of pay averaging up to 50 cents an hour less than those paid in the base metal and uranium mines. Obviously no such labour supply was available in Canada, or indeed anywhere else where people knew the score so far as employment in the mining industry was concerned. I am informed that about three months ago the gold mining companies sent representatives to Europe to import necessary miners to work under those conditions. I have also been reliably informed that one of the men who went to Europe was Mr. William Ramsay, the manager of the unemployment insurance commission at Kirkland Lake.
On this account the gold mines are now being operated with older miners. 1 am told that the average age of miners in the gold mining industry in Kirkland Lake is now in excess of 40 years. These miners are held captive by their investment in homes and by the fact that mining operators will not hire men over 40 years of age. I understand it is the intention of these mines to operate with these men, in some cases plus labour imported

from Europe which is willing to work for the lower wage scales provided in the unorganized mines. I understand it is difficult to organize some of these submarginal gold mines because the union cannot offer the men very much in the way of hope for better wage scales and working conditions.
I suggest that the time has come to consider the present distinction between base metal mines and gold mines as being artificial. In our opinion it should be somewhat along the line of profitable and non-profitable mines. I must admit that I am not aware of the details of conditions in northern Ontario, although I am completely at home in the southeastern portion of British Columbia and understand mining conditions there, but I have received my information from what I consider to be most responsible and reliable sources. I understand that there is a large iron prospect at Boston Creek in the Kirkland Lake area which is undeveloped. I wonder whether the government has given consideration to amending this act to provide more flexibility in its administration and purposes and to permit assistance to such developments, either by way of loan or by way of the form of assistance now provided by the act.
In our opinion this act can be effectively administered only as a result of co-operation and a study of the situation in total in the mining industry by the Department of Finance, the Department of Labour and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. We in this group are firmly of the opinion that the time has come for a co-ordinated approach to this problem by the three departments I have mentioned. We think that is very necessary. We should give consideration to making the act more flexible and more realistic in order to meet a situation which apparently is at least temporary-permanent or permanent-temporary, whichever way you like to put it, and thus be able to deal more effectively with the conditions faced by the miners and the communities concerned.
Before concluding I wish to ask the minister a number of questions which I would appreciate his answering when we reach the committee stage. My first question is this: Is Mr. William Ramsay, who has gone to Europe to recruit labour for the mining industry, still an employee of the federal Department of Labour? My second question is this: Is it the government's policy to continue emergency gold mining assistance to certain mines especially in view of the fact that a labour force made up of young, single immigrants will have almost the same effect on those communities and their property values as would the closing of the mines? These immigrants may be willing to work for these substandard
12, 1956	4975
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act wages, but the purpose of the act is to maintain the communities and the standards of the employees concerned. The effect of the employment of these single immigrants on these communities will be almost identical with that which would follow the closing down of the mines.
These men will live in bunk houses and will only be temporary residents. As soon as they know the score and become aware of Canadian conditions in general they will do the same as did a good many others who came here to work on the farms; they will disappear to more lucrative areas. They live in bunk houses or rent rooms and as temporary residents they will not be purchasing property, nor be investing in the community and, as I said before, will not do anything to stabilize the communities or assure their permanency.
My next question is: what is the attitude of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to the mass importation of European labour to work in marginal gold mines under the circumstances that I have outlined, and what co-operation has the department extended to the gold mining operators who are seeking this immigration from Europe to carry out the work in the gold mines? That question is of considerable interest to a good number of persons who work in the mining industry in northern Ontario.
My last question is: has the government given any thought to forcing mining operators receiving emergency gold mining assistance to hire over-age miners in their own communities when the mines they are working in close down?
Here is the situation that exists. Canadian miners that have been employed in the mining industry all their lives have an average age of over 40 years. If it happens that the mine in which they are working closes down, because the other mining operators would not employ miners over 40 years of age- and I think that is related to pension plans and things of that sort-then these good Canadian citizens find themselves out of employment, with their investment in homes and so on in the mining community concerned, while at the same time immigrants are brought in from Europe to take the employment that they otherwise could obtain. We think it would be a wise policy on the part of the government to insist that the mining operators who are accepting gold mining assistance give employment to these miners even though they are over 40 years of age, by some special arrangement.
We think it is most unfortunate that these good Canadian miners should be out of employment and the vacancies taken by miners being brought into this country under these
4976	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act [DOT]conditions. We are not opposed to planned immigration and the location of immigrants according to proper circumstances and conditions, but I for one am very much opposed to bringing in immigrants from Europe to take the positions that are vacant while under certain circumstances Canadian citizens are unemployed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO THE YEARS 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
This short bill No. 417 simply extends for two years more the bill that was introduced last year. As has been pointed out, there is no change in principle nor in application of the emergency gold mining assistance to the problem of the gold mining communities.
Last year, as reported at pages 2177 to 2184 of Hansard, I dealt at very considerable length with the economics of the gold mining industry and all the social consequences of the problems of that industry and the gold mining communities and the miners and citizens who live and have lived there, many of them for a generation or more, and are firmly established there, in considering the proposal that was then before the house in regard to reducing the assistance to be paid. I consider that no good purpose would be served in repeating what was said there, as it is readily available in Hansard for anyone who wishes to reconsider the problem with which we were faced a year ago.
I urged at that time that the government reconsider its proposal to reduce the amount of emergency gold mining assistance, but the government proceeded with its program. The minister expected that there would be a


reduction in the over-all payment of assistance from $16 million in 1954-in fact it turned out to be about $16,300,000 in 1954 -to $11 million in 1955. Now, in introducing this extension of the policy, the minister is able to tell us that in fact the total payment in 1955 will be in the neighbourhood of $9,300,000, about $1,700,000 less than he estimated when he introduced this policy to the house a year ago, so that in effect the reduction in payment to the gold mining industry is from $16,300,000 to $9,300,000 in one year, with anticipated further reductions over the next three years of the life of this program. That is a reduction of 43 per cent, and it is a very considerable and substantial reduction.
How the government justified the reduction which was made last year was more than I could see from anything that was said, except on the ground of saving an immediate outlay of funds. I endeavoured to show the importance of the industry at that time, with its 18,500 workers, its great communities, well established permanent communities, many of them based entirely on the gold industry, with no possible alternative means of support. In that connection I suggest to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) that it would be desirable for him to visit some of these communities because his idea of what they are is somewhat removed from the facts as found in the gold mining report made by the committee in Ontario, at least the facts as they apply in the province of Ontario, of which I believe he was speaking.
I commend this report to the members of the house. It has been mentioned already by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mrs. Shipley). It was the report of a committee of inquiry into the economics of the gold mining industry in 1955, under the chairmanship of Professor F. A. Knox of Queen's University, and with a very competent committee supporting him. An interim report was made last year, and the final report this year. It is interesting to note the composition of the mining group in the Ontario camps. I think the Porcupine camp is the largest and probably the most representative. In that camp, according to the table on page 83 of the report, there were 6,135 men who were reported for the purposes of this committee, and the number of Canadian-born were 3,556. That is a little more than half. Of these, 942 were French speaking and 2,614 were English speaking. Then I come to those who came from abroad, and here is where the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) would be interested from the point of view of verifying the statements which he was making on

"very good" authority. Those from the British Isles numbered 598 while those from east and south Europe numbered 1,728 which shows that the miners who are there are about half newcomers and about half Canadian born.
Even more interesting are the figures on recent arrivals. Immigrants into that camp since 1945 numbered only 452, of those who reported, less than 10 per cent, and since 1950 there have been only 305. That does not show any great change in the composition of the miners in the camps. The ages were also the subject of a study made by the same committee, and I think members might be interested in the ages of the miners in the Porcupine camp because after all this assistance is a guarantee that these men will be able to continue to work in the jobs they have known and where their homes are, where their children go to school and where they expect to live their entire lives.
Under 19 years of age there were only 185. From 20 to 24 years there were 1,053, from 25 to 34 years there were 3,064 and from 35 to 44 years 2,801. That is about the breaking point that the hon. member for Kootenay West suggested. Up to that point we cover substantially more than half of the miners. From 45 to 54 there are only 2,451, and in the group from 55 to 59 there are only 798. That is by way of a description of these communities and the consideration of the social consequences of this legislation.
Apart from the industry itself, gold is of great importance in our economy. It has a permanent value, and I do not need to repeat what I have said before and what has been said by others on that score. The Ontario report at page 67 may be some authority for the relative importance of gold, the continuing importance of gold, and I will read one paragraph which illustrates the point to which the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) drew attention earlier.
During the depression of the li)30's gold exports were of considerable importance in our balance of payments. In the two years 1935-37, for instance, gold exports averaged 14-5 per cent of our total merchandise exports, the average gold export being $132 million and merchandise exports $909 million. In the first two years of the second world war, before other methods were devised to finance essential war imports from the United States, the Canadian government urged all-out gold production from the mines.
It is not likely that proportion will return but that illustrates the great role that gold played, as anyone who lived through that period, particularly in Ontario, knows, in maintaining the stability of the economy.
Then, the place of gold as a monetary reserve is, I submit, a basic consideration in support of an advanced policy of assistance.
12, 1956	4977
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act The gold reserves must be placed opposite the inflow of capital because the capital which comes into Canada, which we all welcome, and which is playing such a part in the building up of our resources, is all exportable again. As I pointed out last year, in the period of emergency gold mining assistance $3 billion in new capital had come into Canada in the same period all of which, if it were demanded, would have to be paid back. In consequence the establishment of a substantial reserve in an acceptable form of money, namely, gold, is the necessary counterpart of our policy of permitting the free investment of foreign capital in Canada.
In addition, gold mining is not simply an industry to itself. As the minister has recognized, gold mining has led to some of the forms of mining which are now more profitable such as the base metal mining which is being carried on today to an ever-increasing degree. It was gold that gave the boost which started hard rock mining in this country and exploration for base metals. Gold mines have played a very substantial part in financing base metal mines and have supplied the engineers, the technique, the capital, everything necessary for the great expansion in the base metal industry. They have played and are playing an important part not only in the production of gold but in the mineral development of Canada.
What has been the effect of the policy which the minister introduced a year ago? His own statement indicates that the industry is a failing industry, and I think that is the most important consideration before the house in determining whether this policy should be renewed just as it is or whether the assistance ought to be increased, as was urged last year. It is a failing industry. It is true that total ounces produced last year were slightly greater than the year before and to that extent there is cause for satisfaction, but that production is at the expense of the future. The minister admits that five of the lode mines, as opposed to placer mines, have suspended operations in the course of the year. One was absorbed by the parent company and one new mine was opened. The net loss is five of the lode mines out of a total of about 54, I believe, which are receiving assistance.
The minister, to use his own words, says that other gold mines are in a life and death struggle for existence. That does not indicate a very healthy industry to anyone who has heard him support continuation of this policy in its present form and the results it has achieved over the past year. In addition, the minister says that some of the mines may close. After the present act expires it is
4978	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act anticipated that 18 to 20 mines may close permanently.
A more serious consequence of the present condition of the industry is that there is very little prospecting and there are very few new mines being discovered, opened up and operated. In the period from 1941 to 1955 the number of mines in operation has been reduced by more than half, and one has only to project these trends into the future to see that the gold mining industry, if it depends on this temporary assistance and is not restored by a more permanent solution, is doomed to disappear in Canada.
The cost of what the government has done has been pretty well reviewed by the hon. member for Eglinton. I should like to point out to the house that the total cost of this assistance from its inception in 1948 is only $90 million. That $90 million has accounted for the production of $950 million worth of gold so that putting it at the highest the cost of putting into being gold which would not otherwise have existed as an asset in the Canadian treasury has been only 10 per cent of the amount of newly-mined gold in this country over that period. That is a very small premium for the insurance which this gold gives as part of our reserves.
In the period of the subsidy our reserves have increased by about the amount of the newly-mined gold, although not quite as much. In December of 1954 our reserves stood at $1,072 million, as has been said, and at the end of the last calendar year they stood at $1,134 million, an increase of $62 million in the course of the calendar year. The costs I have put at 10 per cent, being the relation of the assistance to the total production. But those costs are offset by a great many forms of taxation which bring back into the treasury a good part of the emergency gold mining assistance. Those are direct taxes on the profits of the mines and also taxes on the mining communities where the emergency gold mining assistance is largely put into circulation. Hence the net cost of providing Canada with this kind of insurance against its external obligations in the form of a vast reserve of gold, now well over $1 billion, is negligible as compared with its permanent value. In addition, this industry lends itself particularly to assistance because it is not a competitive industry. There is only one purchaser of its product, basically, and that is the government. Therefore in subsidizing in an indirect way by public funds we are not interfering with other enterprise. Furthermore, there is no danger of overproduction which is another hazard of a subsidy as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has found out to his great embarrassment.


The net cost then is small in proportion to the values which one can see from the application of this policy. I have only two criticisms to make. The first is the criticism that I made last year, namely that the minister was wrong in reducing the assistance. If he had not reduced it the production would undoubtedly have been greater. Not only would some of the mines which have gone out of production have stayed in production but there would have been more incentive for exploration and the development of new mines. I know of gold mines where there are substantial tonnages of ore waiting to be mined when it is profitable to do so. Hence I think it is fair to say that the production of gold, the amount of gold put into being and flowing into the reserves of this country, would have been greater had the assistance not been reduced. There is a marginal point where gold ore will be left in the ground if the assistance is withdrawn. The minister knows that very well.
Then the other criticism-and it has already been voiced-is that the government does not appear to have attempted to find a permanent solution. At least, if they have done so, it has been kept quiet. I should like to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) what approach he has made to the international monetary fund or bank, whichever institution has authority in these matters, or what efforts have been made in international consultation to find a means of increasing the price of gold. The minister last year accused me of being in favour of gambling with public funds, I believe, when I said there was a real possibility that these reserves which he is providing for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) in the form of $1 billion in gold valued at $35, might very readily by the stroke of an international agreement become worth another $1 billion if the price of gold were doubled, as has been done in the past and as, I am sure, will be done again one day, because these things have a habit of recurring under similar conditions. Hence it is reasonable to expect that there can be no loss on this gold which the government is helping to produce. It is also reasonable to expect that there may very readily be a substantial profit to the Canadian economy and the Canadian people as a whole; and in the meantime there is a substantial benefit to those who are directly engaged in this industry as miners and their families and those who serve the mining communities.
On those two points I suggest that the government has failed in its duty. Of course I cannot complain of the fact that the act is being extended for a further two years because it is obviously of great benefit to the country and to the gold mining industry

particularly; it is of great benefit to know two years in advance just what the course of events will be. I therefore do not propose to vote against this bill but I would have liked this year-as I would have liked it last year -to see the assistance kept at the level at which it had been established. I should like to know what the government has been doing, or what effort it has made to have a review of the price of gold among the nations of the world who are concerned with it. It is 10 years since the Bretton Woods agreements were made and in all conscience that is enough time to know what the consequence of that $35 fixed price of gold has been to the great gold-producing countries like Canada, South Africa and others.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few brief words about this matter. I wonder whether all hon. members in their mind's eye can go back to the beginnings of this industry in Ontario. Many of them are not old enough perhaps to go back to the time when the Ontario government first started to build the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway in northern Ontario and to know what happened. First it opened the great town of Cobalt which became a great silver centre which remained for many years. Then as those with pioneering spirits started to get ahead of the railway, the first thing we knew gold was discovered up in Timmins. It must have struck a tremendous chord with everyone in Canada when it became known that gold had been discovered in northern Ontario. First there was just a little camp, with a few tents and someone who had a general store. Then as time went on these things grew, and finally a great big town appeared. Then we had gold discovered in Kirkland Lake. I can remember, back in 1922, getting off the train at Swastika. You had to get the old bus and go six miles from there into Kirkland Lake. It was a town of shacks at that time. People were buying Teck-Hughes stock at 15 cents a share; and if they bought it, they did not know where they were going to sell it. Now when you walk into Kirkland Lake, what do you find? It is a terrific town, one that you can be proud of. Then you went over to Larder Lake, Elk Lake and so on and so forth. This gold mining industry of ours just seemed to cause towns to spring up all over the place. As has been mentioned already, back in the early thirties, there was one place in Canada to which every traveller wanted to go to sell his merchandise, namely to northern Ontario because that is where business was good. Why? Just because of the gold mines.
Then along came the first increase in price, and away things went again. Prospectors 67509-316
12, 1956	4979
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act went out looking for more gold, this precious metal which meant so much to everyone. Then all at once what happened? World war II came along. The cost of everything started to go up. Here was an industry with a level selling price and the cost of everything going up. Miners had to be paid more money; and it was right and just that they should. Merchandise cost more; machinery cost more; everything cost more. But the poor mining companies had a ceiling on what they could get for their merchandise. Things became so bad that eventually you brought in this Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act in order to help many of these companies out.
It is said that this is a failing industry. That is a terrible word for us in Canada to use in talking about any industry. I do not think it is a failing industry. There is just one thing that keeps any industry from failing and that is salesmanship. All right. What have we to sell? We have a couple of things to sell. One of them is up to the government. They have to sell to the United States of America the idea that the price of gold must be either "upped" or freed. There is no question about that. We do not know how hard the government is going after it, or just how sincere their intentions are. I realize and understand that the United States is worried perhaps a little bit, or perhaps a lot, because we do not know what this might do to Russia. We hear they could be the second largest gold-producing country in the world. These are things that we do not know at the moment.
As I said on the resolution stage of this bill, those who are allowed to get the subsidy are not allowed to sell gold on the free market. That is something that I just cannot understand. I mentioned it before. If we allow everyone to sell on the free market and they are getting $3.48 subsidy now, and if they got an extra $2.48, the government would have to pay them only $1 an ounce when they produced the ore, if their sales averaged that.
I have another thought in mind for doing that. It would mean that all the gold mining companies could get together and have a sales force to start to re-educate the people of Canada about gold, what gold is and what they could do with gold. Hon. members can recall, as I can, when we used to get $10 gold pieces and $5 gold pieces for gifts and we used to get them as presents, and so on and so forth. But there are many people living in Canada today who have never seen a $5 or a $10 gold piece. Why can these gold mining companies not get together and build up a sales force and re-educate the Canadian people in the use of gold and perhaps in other ways? Let us go back and
4980	HOUSE OF
Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act see what happened to the nickel companies. You know what they did. They built up a research department and they are finding more and more uses for nickel. Why are the gold mining companies not encouraged to do that sort of thing instead of being left to themselves? Why should we say to them, "We will give you so many dollars. Do not go above that. We are going to give you your subsidy, but also let you go out on the free market." In case it does not work out and they lose their subsidy the minister says to me that they can come back on January 1 or July 1. I know all that, sir; but in the meantime, how much money have they lost?

speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Is the hon. member aware that on the so-called free market the price of gold is less than $35 an ounce?

I realize that, but perhaps on the free market they could get more than that. That is what I am trying to tell the minister. I know you can buy gold at the mint, too, but all you can get there is a gold brick. You cannot go and get a $10 gold piece, or anything like that. You might be able to get $38, $39 or $40 an ounce for units of small articles that could be sold. There is no reason why that could not be done. If the government will only try to get the United States to increase the price of gold or let it go free, it would be a great help. Once again, we are hamstrung by our neighbours to the south. This is an actual fact. We must admit that. We know that Canada could not raise the price up to $50 or $60 an ounce or every country in the world would be sending their gold here; that is certain. The United States is different because they are the biggest purchaser of gold in the world.
Gold is something that we have to keep because of the fact that all these towns and all the people that are in these towns and all the industries that are tied up and allied with it are dependent on gold. You know, there is not a prospector today out looking for gold. I can imagine there is all kinds of gold in Ontario, but it does not pay. Suppose a prospector finds a great strike of gold, who wants it? I can remember back in 1936, I think it was when they made the strike in the O'Brien mine in Cadillac township. It was free gold; it was not too big. I was down in the mine; I saw it. It was the most gorgeous looking thing you ever saw. It was solid gold about the size of the top of this desk. There is lots more of it around this country. I have staked hundreds and hundreds of claims in my time. I never got a big one. Like every prospector, you always look for some bonanza somewhere along the line. But now no one is encouraged to go out and look for gold at all. I always say


this: no matter where you are in the world, if you have gold you can do business and trade. That is what brought this country to where it is today. I just hope we can continue on to do that.
Certainly, we must have this subsidy. There is not any question about that. I still think that the minister should allow every mine, whether they are getting the subsidy or not, to try to see what they can do to develop a free market for gold. They have no sales force. That is one thing the gold mining companies never had, is sales force. They just shipped it down to the mint. That is all they had to worry about. So long as they had insurance on the bullion coming from the mine to Ottawa they were through. That is all the selling they had to do. I think they should get together and start a research and sales department, and I think everyone would be surprised at what could be done.
Of course, I am going to vote for this bill. There is nothing else one can do. It is a help; it is not enough. But I do hope-and I want to repeat this once again-that the minister will seriously consider allowing all the mines to go into the free market regardless of whether or not they are getting the subsidies. If they make more than the present price it will come off the subsidy. It will not entail any bookkeeping work. They must keep track of their sales anyway; therefore the extra bookkeeping work, if there is any, would be small.
